source.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
source.authors: Ruben Härle; Felix Friedrich; Manuel Brack; Stephan Wäldchen; Bjorn Deiseroth; P. Schramowski; K. Kersting

record.tranche_reason: The study measures monosemanticity of language-model SAE latent features using its own Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), rather than measuring individual MLP neurons with the original methods.
record.gate_note: The study reports FMS results for vanilla and guided SAEs, comparisons across FMS settings, and SAE-Bench capability comparisons. It does not measure the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures how monosemantic sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents are, using its own Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS). SAE latents are not the neurons of vision models or language-model MLPs, so this is a related but different construct. Its main comparison is its own supervised method (G-SAE), which deliberately forces one latent per labelled concept, against a vanilla SAE. That is a report of its own method's performance, not a measurement of polysemanticity arising in a network's neurons, or of how architecture, activation function or training changes the share of polysemantic neurons. Varying FMS@1 versus @5 and arithmetic versus harmonic means is a sensitivity check on a score for SAE latents. It is not a test of whether neuron polysemanticity depends on the part of the activation range examined or on explanation scoring.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that vanilla SAEs lack reliable monosemanticity and that G-SAE raises FMS across toxicity, style and privacy concepts without hurting SAE-Bench capabilities. They report better detection and steering, and that G-SAE also works as post-hoc finetuning of a pretrained SAE. Table 2 shows that post-hoc finetuning gives higher FMS but worse CE and MSE than the pretrained SAE, notably for privacy.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces FMS and supervised Guided Sparse Autoencoders rather than reproducing the original neuron-visualization or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: FMS results depend on the scoring setting (@1 versus @5); reported monosemanticity also differs between G-SAE pretraining and post-hoc finetuning and across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla SAE latents on Llama3-8B's residual stream are weakly monosemantic: average FMS@1 0.27, and a pretrained EleutherAI SAE scores 0.34. Concepts spread over many latents; a vanilla SAE needs about 41 features on average to match G-SAE's single-feature accuracy. Concept-supervised G-SAE roughly doubles FMS (0.52) with comparable SAE-Bench scores.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised SAE latents in LLMs spread labelled concepts across many features, and supervising SAE training on concept labels concentrates each concept in one latent.

record.problems: The study measures supervised concept detection in SAE latent features rather than counting polysemantic MLP neurons or measuring responses to unrelated inputs. FMS depends on the selected classifier and score settings; the paper notes conceptual granularity and residual activation in semantically neighboring concepts. Some table values are flattened in the supplied text, so no uncertain Shakespeare FMS numbers are assigned.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numeric rows were extracted from the flattened Table 1 because the supplied text does not reliably map its Shakespeare values to the FMS@1 and FMS@5 columns. Other SAE-Bench metric-by-metric values in Appendix G are not separate monosemanticity outcomes.

untested.parts: MLP neurons of language models are not measured; only SAE latents on the residual stream.
Superposition as the cause is not tested.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization or training noise without capacity pressure.
The model's own architecture, activation function or regularization is not varied. Only SAE training is supervised.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not reassessed.
Neuron activation ranges and explanation scoring are not compared. The study only varies its own FMS settings on SAE latents.

record.verdict_notes: This is an SAE-method paper. Its 'monosemanticity' refers to dictionary latents against labelled concepts, measured with a classifier-based score. It is not about neuron polysemanticity in the model. The reader's V5 and V7 verdicts are removed.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test neurons in image classifiers or InceptionV1.
It studies SAE latent features, not MLP neurons, and does not measure responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
It does not test superposition or capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
It does not test whether initialization, regularization, or training noise cause polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.

It compares vanilla SAEs with guided, supervised SAEs and evaluates SAE capability; it does not compare SoLU, modern convnets, or the specific architecture and activation-function changes listed in the version.
It does not reassess canonical polysemantic neurons for a shared feature such as pose.
It varies FMS scoring settings, including @1 and @5, but does not compare activation ranges or alternative explanation systems.
